tasks.short: Complete layouts and write typography instructions

steps.what: Paste repeated items into the layouts
Complete layouts the table could not place
Write typography instructions to prepare materials

loop.output: instruction lines each naming a style and a size
loop.check: Every line names a type style and a size from the fields
loop.stop: One pass; leave a blank line where a size is missing
loop.why_not_simpler: How the type should feel is not a field lookup

steps.what: Check the layouts against the printing rules
Approve typography instructions on marked layouts
Send approved materials for typesetting or printing

tasks.design: Repeated items with coordinates are pasted into the layouts from a {SPREADSHEET}. The art director completes the layouts the table cannot place and writes typography instructions in {DOCS}. A checker compares the file with printing rules and does not approve it. The art director approves the instructions, including marks on any model-made image, and only then are the materials sent for typesetting or printing.
tasks.previous_blocker: Standing items and type instructions were redone by eye on every page, with no separate rule check.
tasks.enabler_now: Repeated items can carry an asset id and coordinates, and type style and size can be fields.
tasks.still_hard: Finishing an unusual layout and judging the type are still the art director's work.
tasks.human_edge: The art director completes the layouts and approves the typography instructions. The rule report does not.

ambition.what: Send typography instructions when the layout is complete, not in a later cleanup pass

tasks.altitude: Repeated paste and the rule list move. Completing the layout and signing the type stay. The art director can hold a file the checker could not read.

reach.task: Typeset from the signed typography instructions
reach.learn: Which instructions are signed and which print mismatches remain

evidence.claim: Paste-up is still making a page. Only items with coordinates are mechanical. Typography instructions and the approval stay with the person.

Digest [S2] and [S3] describe a design tool that drafts from a prompt and a campaign-layout tool that fills locked template areas. A person still approves the layout. A filled frame is not the approved design.
Digest [S5] says a prepress checker compares a file to print rules and reports each mismatch. It does not decide the design.
Digest [S9] and [S10] describe EU transparency duties for synthetic media. A person confirms the mark on a model-made image before the materials go out.
Digest [S11] reports that campaign images often omit that mark. The mark check is mandatory in this design.

assumptions: Focal role is the art director. The task ends when signed materials are sent to typesetting or printing. The press visit is a different task.

Input contract: layout id, asset id, x, y, type style, type size, model-made yes or no, mark status. Producer is the art director from the signed spec. Rows with no coordinates are left for the art director and not placed by guess.
Use the template placement and the existing print profile before custom code. An unusual layout is finished by hand.
unknowns: What share of items already have coordinates.
Whether type size is stored as a field or only as drawn type.
research_questions: How many items on a typical layout are repeated with coordinates?
How often does the rule check fail a file the art director would have sent?

already_counted.description: Completing unusual layouts stays with the art director
Approving typography instructions stays with the art director

incremental.description: Add placement columns when a new repeated item type appears

approvals.approved_version: typography instructions signed for these layouts

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes almost no item has coordinates, so paste stays manual and only the rule report is new. The high case assumes repeated items place cleanly, while unusual layouts, the typography instructions and the approval still take their time. The press run is not counted as saved.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Design interfaces for multimedia products and devices

steps.what: Describe the devices, games and products
Draft interfaces for the multimedia products

loop.output: interface frames labelled draft and citing a device id
loop.check: Each frame cites a device id and is labelled draft
loop.stop: One pass; stop if no device id is present
loop.why_not_simpler: The interaction idea is not a template fill

steps.what: Conceptualize interfaces with the product team
Approve the design of interfaces for these devices
Clear rights and marks before interfaces are shared
File the interface concept cleared for sharing

tasks.design: The product lead describes the devices, games and products in {DOCS}. A bounded draft proposes interfaces and labels them draft. The art director conceptualizes the interfaces with the team, approves the design, and clears rights and marks before anything is shared. The concept is filed in {CMS} with content-credential metadata. A generated frame is not the approved design.
tasks.previous_blocker: Device limits were verbal, so a concept could not show which screen size it was for.
tasks.enabler_now: Device, screen size and product id can be fields the draft must cite.
tasks.still_hard: What the interface should be is still a design judgement made with people.
tasks.human_edge: The art director approves the interface concept and does not treat a generated screen as owned.
tasks.altitude: The first frames take less blank-page time. The concept session and the two sign-offs stay. The art director can block a share while rights or marks are open.

reach.task: Build only from the interface concept that was cleared
reach.learn: Which devices the concept covers and whether rights and marks are done

evidence.claim: Interface concepts are worked out with other people. A draft can start from device fields. It is not the design.
Digest [S2] and [S3] describe design-tool generation and a campaign-layout product. A person still approves. A generated frame is not the approved design.
Digest [S8] is a commentary that generative tools change craft and that a person still directs the work. It is not a measured saving.
Digest [S12], [S13] and [S14] say copyright in a model-made image is unsettled. The art director does not treat a generated image as owned, and a person clears rights before external use.
Digest [S9] and [S10] describe EU transparency duties for synthetic media. A person confirms the mark before a model-made image goes out.
Digest [S11] reports that campaign images often omit that mark. The mark check is mandatory in this design.
Digest [S1] says content-credential metadata can be attached to a creative file. That is metadata, not a judgement that the interface is good.

assumptions: Focal role is the art director. The task ends when the cleared concept is filed. Building the product is out of scope.

Input contract: product id, device id, screen size, game or product type, model-made yes or no. Producer is the product lead. Blank device ids are not guessed; the art director types them and marks the row manual.
Use the document template before custom code. Nothing is shared outside until rights and marks are confirmed.
unknowns: Whether these concepts are shown only inside the firm.
Which screens are model-made rather than drawn.
research_questions: How often is a concept shared before rights are cleared?
How often does the team reject the drafted frames entirely?

already_counted.description: Concept session time stays with the art director
Design approval of the interfaces stays

incremental.description: Add a device field when a new screen size becomes common
Product lead corrects a device id the form rejected

approvals.approved_version: interface design approved for these devices
rights cleared and marks confirmed on this concept
the same rights and mark record

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes device limits stay verbal, so the draft rarely cites a field and the art director concepts from a blank page. The high case assumes a usable draft but the session, the design approval and the rights check still happen. Product engineering is not counted as saved.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

steps.what: Set sequence and timing rows for the story
Draft detailed storyboards for television production

loop.output: frames labelled draft, one per sequence number
loop.check: Each frame cites one sequence number from the sheet
loop.stop: One pass; skip a row with no duration
loop.why_not_simpler: The story development is not a row in the sheet

steps.what: Prepare storyboards showing the story development
Approve storyboards once rights and marks are clear
Send the storyboards to television production

tasks.design: Sequence and timing sit on a {SPREADSHEET}. A bounded pass may draft storyboard frames in {DOCS} and label them draft. The art director prepares the storyboards showing the story development, then approves them only when rights are clear and any model-made frame is marked. That version is sent for television production and filed in {CMS} with content-credential metadata.
tasks.previous_blocker: Timing lived in the margins of drawings, so a frame could not be checked against a sequence number.
tasks.enabler_now: Sequence number, start time and duration can be rows a frame must cite.
tasks.still_hard: How the story develops is still drawn and judged by the art director.
tasks.human_edge: The art director prepares the storyboards and does not send a generated frame as the approved board.
tasks.altitude: Timing rows are easier to line up. Drawing and the release decision stay. The art director can hold a board whose frames do not match the sequence.

reach.task: Schedule the television shoot from the signed storyboards
reach.learn: Which sequence is approved and whether marks and rights are done

evidence.claim: Storyboards are a sequence of frames plus timing. The timing can be rows. The frames and the story are still made by the art director.
Digest [S8] is a commentary that generative tools change craft and that a person still directs the work. It is not a measured saving.
Digest [S1] says content-credential metadata can be attached to a creative file. That is metadata, not a judgement that the storyboard is good.
Digest [S9] and [S10] describe EU transparency duties for synthetic media. A model-made image or video is marked before it goes out, and a person confirms the mark.
Digest [S11] reports that campaign images often omit that mark. The mark check is mandatory in this design.
Digest [S12], [S13] and [S14] say copyright in a model-made image is unsettled. The art director does not treat a generated frame as owned, and a person clears rights before external use.

assumptions: Focal role is the art director. The task ends when the storyboards are sent to television production. Shooting the programme is out of scope.

Input contract: story id, sequence number, start time, duration, model-made yes or no. Producer is the art director from the script note. A frame with no sequence number is not drafted and is drawn by hand.
Use the sheet's own columns before custom code. A generated frame stays labelled draft until the art director approves the boards.
unknowns: Whether television production is inside the firm or a supplier.
What share of frames are model-made.
research_questions: How often do frame counts disagree with the timing rows?
How often is a board sent with no mark on a model-made frame?

already_counted.description: Preparing the storyboards stays with the art director
Approval of storyboards, rights and marks stays

incremental.description: Adjust timing columns when a new programme format is added

approvals.approved_version: storyboards approved with rights cleared and marks confirmed

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes there is no timing sheet, so frames are still planned on paper and the draft does not run. The high case assumes clean timing but the art director still prepares and approves the storyboards. The television shoot is not counted as saved.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Negotiate services with printers and estimators

steps.what: List the services that must be performed
Return an estimate for those services
Negotiate with printers and with estimators
Determine which services will be performed
File the services the negotiation settled

tasks.design: The art director lists the services to be performed in {DOCS}. The estimator returns a price by {EMAIL} against that list, compared on a {SPREADSHEET}. The art director negotiates with the printers and the estimators, determines which services will be performed, and files that decision in {PROJECT}. The negotiation stays in the room.
tasks.previous_blocker: Services were described differently in each mail, so quotes could not be lined up.
tasks.enabler_now: A service id lets an estimate point at the same line the art director asked for.
tasks.still_hard: What to accept, and at what price, is still a negotiation with people.
tasks.human_edge: The art director determines which services will be performed. The estimate does not.
tasks.altitude: Lining up quotes takes less reconstruction. The negotiation stays. The art director can refuse a decision that names a service not on the list.

reach.task: Perform only the services named in the filed decision
reach.learn: Which services were accepted and which estimates were declined

evidence.claim: Negotiating print services is a conversation with suppliers. A shared service list can line up quotes. It does not choose the supplier.

assumptions: Focal role is the art director. The task ends when the service decision is filed. Attending the press is a different task.

Input contract: job id, service id, quantity, estimate amount, supplier id. Producer of the list is the art director. Producer of the amount is the estimator. A quote with no service id is set aside and matched by hand.
Use the sheet's own columns to line up quotes before custom code. This is not a room plan, so no space-planning modeller is used.
unknowns: Whether more than one printer quotes the same service.
Who may accept a price when the art director is away.
research_questions: What share of quotes arrive with no service id?
How often does the negotiation drop a service that was on the list?

already_counted.description: Negotiation time with printers and estimators stays
The service decision stays with the art director

incremental.description: Add a service line when a new press extra becomes common
Estimators resend quotes that lacked a service id

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes quotes stay as free-text mail, so the art director still rebuilds the comparison. The high case assumes lined-up quotes but the negotiation and the service decision still take their full time. The print cost itself is not counted as saved.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The week keeps typography, interface judgement, storyboards and printer negotiation, and spends less time on repeated paste-up, timing rows and quote chasing.
reach: Printers receive typography instructions and a file already checked against print rules.
The product lead receives an interface concept only after rights and marks are cleared.
Estimators can see the service list before the negotiation, which itself stays in the room.
skills_to_grow: Write typography instructions a typesetter can follow without another meeting.
Mark a model-made storyboard frame before it goes to production.
Separate a printer's price from the services actually accepted.
role.ambitious_version: Typography goes to the printer with a rule report, and no model-made storyboard or interface leaves without a rights check and a mark.
